entities.summary:
Marcus of Viterbo (born c. 1304, died September 12, 1369) emerged as a pivotal figure within the Franciscan Order and the papal curia during the turbulent mid-14th century, a period defined by the Avignon Papacy, the aftermath of the Black Death, and growing European political fragmentation. An Italian Franciscan friar, his career culminated in his election as Minister General of the Order of Friars Minor in 1359 and his elevation to Cardinal Priest by Pope Urban V in 1366. His influence extended across the spiritual and political landscapes of Western Europe, particularly through his administrative leadership of the Franciscans and his crucial diplomatic missions on behalf of the Avignon pontiffs, contributing significantly to papal efforts to maintain authority and stability amidst widespread upheaval.

Elected Minister General at the General Chapter held in Perugia on June 9, 1359, Marcus of Viterbo immediately embarked on a systematic visitation of the Franciscan provinces, endeavoring to restore discipline and unity within an order grappling with internal divisions and the devastating demographic impact of the Black Death. His administrative acumen caught the attention of Pope Urban V, who appointed him as a papal legate to various European courts, including those of France and England, where he sought to mediate peace during the Hundred Years' War. His diplomatic efforts were central to the papacy's broader strategy of reasserting moral and political leadership from Avignon, culminating in his creation as Cardinal Priest of Santa Susanna on September 18, 1366, a testament to his trusted position within the highest echelons of the Church.
